newsitem.title: USA: Gore says SEC,IRS coordinating yield burning plans.
newsitem.headline: Gore says SEC,IRS coordinating yield burning plans.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore said Friday the Securities and Exchange Commission and Internal Revenue Service are in talks about coordinating their enforcement efforts on yield burning, a key state government official said.

Daniel Sprague, executive director of the Council of State Governments, said that at a White House meeting with seven state and local government groups, Gore "expressed sympathy" on Friday for municipalities that say they are getting the brunt of a yield burning problem initiated largely by bond dealers.

Sprague said that Mark Schwartz, president of the National League of Cities, told Gore that issuers feel like they are in a speeding taxicab where the passenger gets hit with a policeman's ticket instead of the cab driver.

"I think he was taken by the analogy," Sprague said of Gore, during a press briefing after Friday's meeting. "He said that story really sharpens the focus for what is at stake here. (He said) I can understand your feelings."
Sprague said Gore then reported that IRS and SEC were in fact "having a dialogue" on how to coordinate their enforcement efforts.

New York Gov. George Pataki, president of the Council of State Governments, told reporters that Gore "seemed responsive" to states' and localities' concerns about yield burning, but made no promises to change the policy on the issue.

"The vice president seemed responsive," Pataki told reporters following the one-hour meeting between Gore and the seven groups on a variety of issues, including yield burning, taxation of Internet use, and reauthorization of federal transportation infrastructure legislation.

"(He) was understanding of the issues that were raised. (But) on none of the issues did he make a promise that he was going to effectuate a particular policy," Pataki said. "I don't think we expected that," Pataki continued. "We merely expected for him to listen to the concerns that states and localities were raising."

The League said in a press statement that "Vice President Gore's response at the meeting Friday was a clear signal that the Treasury Department will become actively involved in examining the enforcement actions proposed by SEC and IRS, and also involving the Justice Dept."
Yield burning refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharged states and localities in recent years for U.S. Treasury securities that they bought to help them refinance outstanding bonds.
In a controversial move last year, the IRS announced that municipalities can avoid having bonds declared taxable by settling any overcharges with the agency now.

But muni groups said that cities and counties were unaware of yield burning. Instead of billing them, IRS and SEC should coordinate efforts and recover U.S. losses from the bond underwriters that engineered the overcharges, groups say.
"The feeling is you don't hold governments responsible when (they relied) on underwriters," Pataki told reporters.
"To the extent that there's a problem, the SEC and IRS should go after those who issued the rulings that everything was in compliance, as opposed to imposing the costs on local governments," he said.
Pataki said he is unaware of any yield burning overcharges owed by New York State.
Schwartz, who is council member of Oklahoma City, said Gore's response is a "great victory and a great hurdle overcome for cities."
"Vice President Gore's message is a very positive signal that cities will not arbitrarily suffer the burden of responsibility for something they did not knowingly do or benefit from," Schwartz said.

Among others attending Friday's meeting were Chicago Mayor Richard Daley, president of the U.S. Conference of Mayors; Michael Hightower, president of the National Asociation of Counties; and Michael Box, Alabama's House majority chairman and president of the National Conference of State Legislatures.
